forces: Woodwinds, percussion, piano, harps, celesta and divided strings; no brass
performers: Philharmonic Symphony Orchestra of London; Artur Rodzinski, conductor
intro: Shostakovich leaves the brass silent and divides the strings into eight parts. The Largo begins as a quiet lament, then finds a terrible force in massed strings, piano and xylophone.

sections.label: A · Eight parts for strings
sections.mNote: Three violin groups, two viola groups and two cello groups

sections.label: B · Flutes above the harp
sections.mNote: One flute, then two, over plucked harp notes

sections.label: C · Strings and woodwinds swell
sections.mNote: Long string lines gather woodwinds around them

sections.label: D · Oboe over trembling violins
sections.mNote: A solo oboe sings above quiet string tremolo

sections.label: Dev · Piano and xylophone
sections.mNote: Hard piano and xylophone attacks reinforce the strings

sections.label: E · Muted strings
sections.mNote: The strings put on mutes after the climax

sections.label: Coda · Harp, violin, then celesta
sections.mNote: The last page pairs celesta with harp harmonics

cues.title: Eight string parts
cues.text: A third group of violins begins the lament in F♯ minor. Shostakovich divides the violins into three groups, the violas and cellos into two each, with the basses below. Their phrases overlap like voices in a choir.
cues.evidence: Shostakovich, Symphony No. 5, Muzgiz full score, plate M. 16313 Г, p. 85, rehearsal 75: eight string staves, with the third violin group beginning the melody. https://imslp.tw/uploads/PMLASIA01319-Shostakovich_Fifth_Symphony%2C__Op__47_-_Full_Score.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Three days at the desk
cues.text: In his introduction to the 1956 score, Shostakovich writes: “I wrote the third part in three days.” He describes a long period of preparation before the music reaches the page. The movement lasts nearly a quarter of an hour here.
cues.evidence: Shostakovich, Introduction to the Score of Symphony No. 5, Muzgiz (1956), quoted by DSCH Publishers: https://shostakovich-en.ru/140en .

cues.title: Flutes above a harp
cues.text: The strings fall silent. A flute sings above the harp’s plucked notes, and a second flute joins it. After so many bowed voices, the harp leaves little spaces around each note.
cues.evidence: Muzgiz full score, p. 88, rehearsals 79–80: flute solo and harp, followed by two flutes; strings resting. https://imslp.tw/uploads/PMLASIA01319-Shostakovich_Fifth_Symphony%2C__Op__47_-_Full_Score.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The strings gather the winds
cues.text: The string lines swell, joined by woodwinds. Shostakovich makes the orchestra cry out while every trumpet, horn and trombone remains silent. The violins have to carry the strain themselves.
cues.evidence: Muzgiz full score, pp. 89–92, from rehearsal 81: growing string and woodwind writing; the Largo has no brass parts. https://imslp.tw/uploads/PMLASIA01319-Shostakovich_Fifth_Symphony%2C__Op__47_-_Full_Score.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Oboe over trembling strings
cues.text: An oboe sings above the violins’ quiet tremolo. The bowing trembles continuously beneath a melody that has to pause for breath. Later, clarinet and flute take their own turns in this exposed space.
cues.evidence: Muzgiz full score, pp. 92–94, rehearsals 84–86: oboe, then clarinet and flute solos over divided strings. https://imslp.tw/uploads/PMLASIA01319-Shostakovich_Fifth_Symphony%2C__Op__47_-_Full_Score.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A cry and a wail
cues.text: After the première the press prints about twenty articles. Most are positive, but Alexander Ostretsov complains that “the pathos of suffering” is in places “taken to a naturalistic cry and wail”.
cues.evidence: DSCH Publishers, work history of Symphony No. 5: about twenty press articles, an overall positive assessment with “quite a number of negative statements”, and Ostretsov’s criticism. Russian text: «пафос страдания в ряде мест доведён до натуралистического крика и вопля» (https://shostakovich.ru/140ru); the English page renders it “the spirit of suffering … raised to a naturalistic shout and howl” (https://shostakovich-en.ru/140en). Our translation follows the Russian.

cues.title: Piano and xylophone bite
cues.text: Piano and xylophone strike into the string lament. Their hard attacks cut across the bowed sound; the cellos drive their line out in force. The brass are still silent.
cues.evidence: Muzgiz full score, pp. 98–99, rehearsal 89: piano and xylophone reinforce the woodwinds and strings. https://imslp.tw/uploads/PMLASIA01319-Shostakovich_Fifth_Symphony%2C__Op__47_-_Full_Score.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Can tragedy be Soviet?
cues.text: In his 1956 introduction to the score, Shostakovich asks whether tragedy belongs in Soviet art and answers yes. He points to Verdi’s and Mozart’s Requiems, whose stern characters fill men’s souls “with courage and the will to struggle”.
cues.evidence: Shostakovich, Introduction to the Score of Symphony No. 5, Muzgiz (1956), quoted by DSCH Publishers: https://shostakovich-en.ru/140en

cues.title: The strings put on mutes
cues.text: After the long outcry, Shostakovich asks the strings to put on mutes. The bow strokes soften, and the opening lament returns in a veiled sound. The score marks it pianissimo.
cues.evidence: Muzgiz full score, p. 105, rehearsals 92–93: withdrawal into strings marked con sordino and pp. https://imslp.tw/uploads/PMLASIA01319-Shostakovich_Fifth_Symphony%2C__Op__47_-_Full_Score.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Harp beside one violin
cues.text: The harp returns to its spare accompaniment. A solo from the second violins answers above the muted strings. What began with a whole group singing now rests with one player.
cues.evidence: Muzgiz full score, pp. 106–107, rehearsal 94 and following: harp, second-violin solo and reduced muted strings. https://imslp.tw/uploads/PMLASIA01319-Shostakovich_Fifth_Symphony%2C__Op__47_-_Full_Score.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Celesta and harp harmonics
cues.text: Celesta and harp harmonics share the final melody. High string harmonics hang above them, thin and pale. Then the strings close the movement with a chord marked morendo — dying away.
cues.evidence: Muzgiz full score, p. 108, rehearsal 96: celesta, harp harmonics, string harmonics and final string chord marked morendo. https://imslp.tw/uploads/PMLASIA01319-Shostakovich_Fifth_Symphony%2C__Op__47_-_Full_Score.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The strings release the melody
transitions.how: The strings hold their last chord and stop. The harp continues alone beneath a flute solo; a second flute joins the first at rehearsal 80. Sustained bowing has been replaced by separate plucked notes under the wind melody.

transitions.title: The strings resume their lament
transitions.how: The flute duet slows and dies away. At A tempo, the divided strings resume their long phrases, beginning quietly and swelling as woodwinds join them. The lower strings carry the bass beneath several independently moving violin lines.
transitions.evidence: Muzgiz full score, pp. 89–92, rehearsal 81 onwards. https://imslp.tw/uploads/PMLASIA01319-Shostakovich_Fifth_Symphony%2C__Op__47_-_Full_Score.pdf

transitions.title: An oboe above the tremolo
transitions.how: The lower strings’ phrases die away under morendo markings. The violins begin a soft tremolo, and an oboe sings above it. The bass falls silent, leaving the solo high over the trembling bows.

transitions.title: Piano and xylophone harden the lament
transitions.how: The strings and woodwinds gather into a crescendo. At the ensuing climax, piano tremolos and xylophone notes reinforce their attack, with the cellos driving the melody below. Shostakovich builds the outcry from strings, reeds and struck notes; the brass have no part.
transitions.evidence: Muzgiz full score, pp. 96–99, leading to rehearsal 89. https://imslp.tw/uploads/PMLASIA01319-Shostakovich_Fifth_Symphony%2C__Op__47_-_Full_Score.pdf

transitions.title: The outcry ends in muted strings
transitions.how: The winds stop after their last emphatic chords. Cellos and basses descend and die away, and the upper strings put on mutes. Their next phrase is marked pianissimo, with the bass held softly beneath it.

transitions.title: The harp picks up the thread
transitions.how: The muted strings diminish, and the harp returns with the plucked accompaniment heard earlier under the flutes. A second-violin solo follows. In the closing bars, celesta and harp harmonics replace the bowed melody while the strings hold high harmonics.

source.title: Symphony No. 5 — Muzgiz M. 16313 Г, historical full score
source.locator: Printed pp. 85–108; PDF pp. 87–110. Brass absent. Three violin groups cannot map literally onto the diagram’s two violin IDs: violins-1/violins-2 jointly represent those groups. Score is public domain in Taiwan, not cleared for EU/US republication; exact performing edition unknown. Selected approximate passage snapshots use cache/analysis/shostakovich-5-largo.txt; source: https://archive.org/details/lp_symphony-no-5-opus-47_dmitri-shostakovich-philharmonic-symphony; not an exhaustive instrument-on/off transcript.

timeline.note: The third violin group initiates the opening, p. 85; its line is represented by violins-2. Lower-string entries follow within the opening passage.
High first-violin line and sustained divided strings, p. 87; broad opening-span placement.
Flute/harp contrast, p. 88/rehearsals 79–80; one flute, then two, with strings initially resting.
First expansion, pp. 89–92; selected active groups in the broad crest, not an exhaustive simultaneous chord inventory.
Oboe over high-string tremolo, p. 92/rehearsal 84; approximately after the 5:04 withdrawal.
Successive clarinet and flute solos over divided strings, p. 94; snapshot covers their passage, not a precisely timed duet.
Second climax, pp. 98–99/rehearsal 89: xylophone represented by percussion; timpani rests on this inspected page. Timing is regional.
Repeated clarinet figures above strongly projected cello material, pp. 100–102/rehearsals 90–91; selected layers in the extended second wave.
Muted string aftermath, p. 105/rehearsal 93; approximately after the 11:00 measured withdrawal.
Harp and second-violin solo with reduced string support, pp. 106–107/rehearsal 94; successive entries grouped into a passage snapshot.
Closing page, p. 108/rehearsal 96: celesta, harp harmonics and string harmonics, followed by the final string sonority. Not an exact celesta entry timestamp.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Philharmonic Symphony Orchestra of London (orchestra), Artur Rodzinski (conductor)
fields.note: Original sleeve and labels establish the displayed credit. Later Westminster reissue documentation and the publisher’s discography identify the orchestra as the Royal Philharmonic Orchestra. That cross-identification is not substituted silently for the original label credit; individual players and soloists are not established.

fields.label: Work version
fields.note: The work and movement are identified, but the exact performing edition is not. The historical score supports broad orchestration and formal observations, not a claim of bar-exact agreement with Rodzinski’s materials. The movement is the entire supplied source track; no local audio edit is made. The set’s finale has a separately disclosed reported cut.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: CiNii’s record for Westminster MVCW-18008 explicitly gives this range; the publisher independently lists the Rodzinski/Royal Philharmonic recording as 1954. Applying those reissue data to this differently credited LP is an inference. No original session ledger or precise movement-by-movement day has been located. 1956 is the selected LP’s publication year, not an invented session date.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: Venue transcribed exactly from the reissue catalogue record. The original LP does not supply a venue. Its linkage to the selected LP is the same qualified inference as the session-date attribution; no more specific hall name is invented.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: Original sleeve and labels; commercially issued Vinyl LP, Made in U.S.A. Sleeve ©1956 Westminster Recording Sales Corp.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: Both forms are visually present on the source object. These identify the selected 1956 issue, not an asserted first edition worldwide. The publisher lists an earlier 1955 Nixa issue of the attributed 1954 performance.

fields.note: Label matrix is legible in the scan. Side 1 contains Moderato/Allegretto; side 2 contains Largo/Allegro non troppo. Take numbers and faint runout/stamper suffixes are unknown and are not guessed.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: The explicit ripping_operator field is credited, not the different uploader/cataloguing operator. A separately named restoration engineer and original recording engineer are unknown.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: LP transfer: Technics SL1200MK5 / Audio-Technica AT95e → Radio Design Labs EZ-PH1 → Focusrite Scarlett 2i2; ArchiveCD 2.2.57lp; source-side 24-bit FLAC and Internet Archive VBR MP3 derivatives
fields.note: Hardware lineage and ripping software are explicit metadata. Original side FLAC tags say Processed by SoX; exact filtering, declicking, gain, speed calibration and derivative segmentation parameters are unknown. The sleeve’s Panorthophonic tape-recording and RIAA-mastering statements concern the original production, not a modern restoration recipe. No local speed correction, normalization, splice or replacement audio was applied.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Not cleared as public domain in the EU or US; composition rights remain separate from the historic recording basis
fields.note: Shostakovich died in 1975. The ordinary EU life-plus-70 calculation runs through 2045; this is not a global clearance or a statement of a US expiry date. IMSLP identifies the work as non-public-domain in the EU and US. The inspected score is territorially hosted as public domain in Taiwan and is cited, not republished. No composition licence is asserted.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 3: territorial EU historic-recording basis; commercial circulation documented by December 1955, selected LP issue dated 1956
fields.note: The original Westminster sleeve/labels and album metadata establish the selected 1956 WN 18001/XWN 18001 issue. A visually inspected High Fidelity review, December 1955, p. 80, already names this London orchestra, Rodzinski, his second recording of the Fifth and Westminster catalogue 18001; the review prints SWN 18001 and erroneously calls the symphony D major, so those details are not silently normalized. The publisher also lists Nixa WLP 20004 in 1955. First lawful publication anywhere before 1963 is the rule; no EU-first-release claim is required or made. source.rights.published 1956 remains a conservative upper bound tied to the selected physical issue, not a first-release date. Even using 1956, the ordinary 50-year recording term had expired before the 2013 extension. US sound-recording status is not established. Complete item metadata, original side-transfer provenance and scans disclose no Creative Commons non-commercial condition or separate upstream digital source. This is not a worldwide public-domain or composition-rights clearance.

sources.title: Symphony No. 5 — inspected historical full score
sources.locator: Printed pp. 85–108; PDF pp. 87–110. 170-page PDF; printed pages are PDF page minus two. Relevant pages were visually inspected for orchestration. This source is a historical score witness, not proof of the exact performing edition or a bar-aligned transcript of the cut finale.

sources.title: Niek Nelissen — Artur Rodzinski, Complete Westminster Recordings
sources.locator: OpusKlassiek, August 2026, Eloquence 484 8489 review. Early paragraph specifies a 37-bar cut in the 1942 Fifth finale; the later Westminster paragraph explicitly states that Rodzinski made the same cut. This supports a reported version difference, not the exact omitted bars or the splice time in this transfer.

sources.title: Museum collection — Pravda, “Muddle Instead of Music,” 28 January 1936
sources.locator: Catalogue of the surviving printed clipping of “Сумбур вместо музыки,” Pravda, 28 January 1936, inventory КП 317996/1315. Establishes the dated public attack, not a decoded political programme for individual notes.

sources.title: Harlow Robinson — Boston Symphony Orchestra work note
sources.locator: Used for Shostakovich’s dates (1906–1975) and the first American performance, Rodzinski/NBC Symphony broadcast, 9 April 1938. The note’s broader interpretive narrative is not treated as proof of private intentions.

sources.title: Testimony — publication and authenticity controversy
sources.locator: 1979 publication by Solomon Volkov, and summary/bibliography of the authenticity dispute, including Laurel Fay. Used only to identify the disputed status of the memoir claim, not as authentication of a Shostakovich quotation.

sources.title: Alex Ross — Unauthorized
sources.locator: The New Yorker, 30 August 2004 / 6 September print issue. Reports Testimony’s 1979 publication, Laurel Fay’s documentary challenge and the continuing distinction between corroborated anecdotes and authenticated authorship. Used as independent evidence of the controversy, not as a settled verdict on every memoir statement or on the finale’s meaning.

composer.epithet: He wrote fifteen symphonies under Soviet rule and signed some of his most personal music with four notes: D–E♭–C–B.
facts: Petrograd Conservatory, 1919–25; Nikolayev for piano, Steinberg for composition
Leningrad from 1937; Moscow from 1943; both posts lost in 1948
D–E♭–C–B♮: DSCH in German note names
Fifteen symphonies and fifteen quartets; operas, concertos and cinema scores
composer.background:
For five weeks the cinema had been showing the same film, and Shostakovich had been playing the same accompaniment. “I’ve even started dreaming about this music,” he wrote from Leningrad to Boleslav Yavorsky on 18 October 1925. He was nineteen. His First Symphony was finished, but a graduation score did not pay the household bills. His father had died three years earlier; accompanying silent films helped keep the family going.

He had been born in St Petersburg in 1906 and learnt the piano from his mother, Sofiya. At the Petrograd Conservatory, which he entered in 1919, Leonid Nikolayev taught him piano and Maximilian Steinberg composition. Alexander Glazunov, the director, recognised his gifts and helped him through his student years. He graduated as a pianist in 1923 and as a composer in 1925.
